en: The Jātaka:
The Ninth Chapter, The Section on Vultures (Gijjhavagga)
10. The Samugga Jātaka “From where have you come, O three men?
Welcome! Come, sit upon these seats.”
"I hope, sirs, that you are well and free from illness;
for it has been a long time since you last came here.
"I alone have arrived here today."
Nor do I have any companion at all;
with what intention, O Lord, did you say this:
“From where indeed have you three people come?”
“You alone and your beloved wife were placed together within this casket;
she was constantly protected by you while still dwelling within your womb.”
“Delighting there with the son of Vāyu.
Having been addressed by the seer in a manner that filled him with awe,
that Dānava vomited up what he had swallowed right there.
He saw his wife, wearing pure garlands,
there delighting with the Son of Vāyu. "O Uggata,
who follows the path of the virtuous, you have seen a beautiful sight!"
Base are those men who have fallen under the sway of women;
they are indeed protected here as if by a living corpse,
while their own wives, being corrupted, take delight in others.
Day and night I have attended upon you,
O ascetic, dwelling with you like a flame in the forest;
yet she, having abandoned the Dhamma, has practiced what is contrary to the Dhamma.
Familiarity with women is a form of non-action.
Thinking "they are staying within my body," I approach them while lacking mindfulness and being unrestrained.
She has abandoned the Dhamma and practiced what is contrary to it;
her nature is one of non-action, and she is intimate with those who are negligent.
How could one trust her, saying, "She is well-guarded"?
In women with manifold thoughts there is no protection; for they are like a precipice falling into the abyss.
He who is heedless therein meets with disaster.
“Therefore, those who move about free from women are indeed happy and free from sorrow;
aspiring for this supreme auspiciousness, [one should dwell thus].”
"One should not cultivate intimacy with women.
Thus ends the tenth Jātaka, the Samugga-jātaka.
